title: Tail latency playground notes (personal)
body:
Quick personal scratchpad for tail-latency experiments (notes, raw numbers, and rough conclusions).

Context:
- Trying to reproduce weird p99 spikes on short-snippet chat workload for hosted API. Seen in prod traces around 1200-1600ms occasionally while p50 ~80ms. Suspect batching + cold KV-cache path interactions.
- Testbed: single-node A100-80GB in staging, runtime build: local-opt-2024-10-29; model: llama-2-13b-v1 (fp16 + actorder), compiled kernels from release-10; test harness: local curl to host + redwood-cli bench.

Experiment notes (raw):
1) Cold vs warmed KV cache (no batching)
- Input: 3-turn chat, avg tokens/request: 120 (prompt+gen), seq_len cap 1024
- Command: redwood-cli infer --model llama-2-13b --tokens 120 --concurrency 1 --batch 1
- Cold run (first after model load): p50 210ms, p90 880ms, p99 1520ms, throughput 6.3 tokens/s
- Warm run (after 100 requests): p50 85ms, p90 180ms, p99 320ms, throughput 24.8 tokens/s
- Notes: large p99 gap on cold; indicates KV-cache warmup cost + occasional kernel path hits.

2) Small batching, frequent delay (attempt to increase throughput while preserving tail)
- Config: max_batch=8, batching_delay_ms=5, concurrency 8
- Observed: p50 120ms, p90 420ms, p99 980ms, throughput 78 tokens/s
- Observations: batching improves throughput but pushes up p99 significantly; spikes correlate with request bursts where one request arrives slightly earlier triggering a small batch and then bigger batch completes later -> head-of-line blocking effect.

3) Continuous batching with adaptive cutoff
- Config: adaptive_batch=true, max_batch=16, cutoff_ms=12
- Observed: p50 95ms, p90 210ms, p99 460ms, throughput 112 tokens/s
- Notes: adaptive cutoff reduced extreme p99 compared to fixed small delay; overall better tradeoff.

4) Tiny inputs (short replies) impact on tail
- Input: avg 8 tokens (short assistant replies) which are latency-sensitive
- With default batching_delay_ms=8: p50 35ms, p90 140ms, p99 720ms
- With delay_ms=0 and max_batch=1 (no batching): p50 28ms, p90 45ms, p99 62ms
- Conclusion: for micro-response workloads, batching can degrade tail badly unless we use smart priority/fast-path.

5) Routing/fallback test (model variants)
- Experiment: route overflow traffic to quantized q4 variant (smaller memory)
- Overflow p99 (hosted): 1.05s, q4 fallback p99: 1.20s but cheaper by ~35% tokens cost
- Takeaway: fallback to cheaper model is OK for throughput but tail may worsen slightly depending on variant kernel compatibility. Worth A/B.

Quick table (summary):
Scenario | p50 | p90 | p99 | tput (tokens/s) | notes
Cold-no-batch | 210ms | 880ms | 1520ms | 6.3 | KV warmup cost
Warm-no-batch | 85ms | 180ms | 320ms | 24.8 | good when hot
Batch 8/delay5 | 120ms | 420ms | 980ms | 78 | head-of-line spikes
Adaptive/16/12 | 95ms | 210ms | 460ms | 112 | best tradeoff seen
Short-resp, no-batch | 28ms | 45ms | 62ms | n/a | micro second-level stable

Observations / hypotheses:
- KV-cache warmup is the dominant factor for first-request p99 — mitigate with pre-warming or serving warm pools.
- Small batching delay helps throughput but can create outliers due to mixed batch sizes and serialization of outputs.
- Adaptive batching (cutoff on both size and time) looks promising for mixed workloads.
- Provide a fast-path for very short responses (bypass batching, prioritize singletons).
- Consider tagging requests with priority classes: realtime vs batchable. Scheduler should avoid head-of-line queuing across classes.

Next steps (actionable):
- Re-run same tests on T4 and DGX (multi-GPU) to check hardware sensitivity (issue ticket).
- Add a microbenchmark that simulates 80% short replies / 20% long replies mix to test adaptive cutoff behavior (write harness).
- Prototype a "warm pool" prefetch: keep 2-3 warm KV contexts per model in each node to reduce cold p99. Measure memory cost.
- Try lowering kernel swap points: force smaller SM kernel selection for short seqs to reduce variance.

Odds-and-ends (notes to self):
- Correlate p99 events with logs: which kernel selected, memcopy timings, GPU utilization. Add trace tags in next run.
- Slack thread: #eng-serving-runtime - add short summary and ping SRE for schedule to test on DGX.

Rough commands used (examples):
- redwood-cli bench --model llama-2-13b --seq 1024 --num-requests 200 --concurrency 8 --max-batch 8 --batch-ms 5
- curl -X POST https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/streams --data '{...}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer ...'

Mini-ascii-chart (p99 progression across runs):
Cold   | ***************** (1520ms)
Warm   | ******** (320ms)
Batch8  | ************* (980ms)
Adaptive| ****** (460ms)

Personal final note: adaptive batching + warm pool looks like the two highest-leverage levers. Will draft mini-proposal for runtime patch (adaptive default + priority fast-path) and attach microbench harness.

-- Evan
